source: USDA ARS Vegetable Crops Research Unit / University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension Commercial Potato IPM
title: Potato Early Blight (Alternaria solani, Ascomycota Pleosporaceae) on Potato and Tomato
content: Potato early blight is the most common and most consistently occurring foliar and tuber disease of cultivated potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) worldwide, affecting all potato-growing regions of North and South America, Europe, Africa, the Middle East, India, China, Southeast Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. The causal organism is the necrotrophic ascomycete filamentous fungus Alternaria solani (Ellis & G. Martin) L.R. Jones & Grout (class Dothideomycetes, order Pleosporales, family Pleosporaceae; teleomorph stage = Lewia infectoria, only rarely observed in nature, not economically important). A second closely related species, Alternaria alternata (Fr.) Keissl. (syn. A. tenuis), often occurs as a secondary saprotrophic invader of senescent potato leaves already weakened by A. solani or abiotic stress, but is not considered a primary early blight pathogen. Annual yield losses of 20-40% are reported in unsprayed susceptible potato cultivars worldwide; in addition to direct foliar yield losses from premature defoliation, tuber infection at harvest causes 5-15% post-harvest storage losses from tuber rot in cool storage, and downgrades processing quality for French fry and potato chip production due to dark necrotic tuber lesions. The name 'early blight' was assigned in the 19th-century North American potato-growing literature because the disease typically appears earlier in the growing season (mid-season, 6-8 weeks after emergence) than the dreaded late blight (Phytophthora infestans, oomycete, which appears later in mid-to-late season under cool wet conditions), although both diseases can and do co-occur on the same potato plants later in the season and often interact synergistically. A. solani also attacks tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.), eggplant (S. melongena), pepper (Capsicum annuum, weakly), and many wild and weedy Solanum species (S. sarrachoides, S. nigrum, S. dulcamara, S. carolinense horsenettle), but potato is the economically most important host. Symptoms occur on leaves, stems, petioles, and tubers. On potato leaves (the most important symptom type), the first symptoms appear on the oldest (lowest-positioned, basal) leaves and lower canopy, beginning as tiny (1-2 mm), circular, dark brown to black necrotic spots. As lesions expand (typically to 5-20 mm diameter, occasionally up to 40 mm under severe pressure), they develop a highly characteristic concentric 'target board' or 'bullseye' zonate pattern of alternating dark and light brown rings (this target-like zonation is the most diagnostic visual feature of early blight lesions, distinguishing them from late blight, Septoria leaf spot, or Verticillium wilt necrotic flecks). Each individual lesion often has a distinct narrow yellow chlorotic halo visible when the leaf is held against the light; the halo is produced by the Alternaria phytotoxin alternaric acid and host phenylpropanoid defense response. Under humid conditions, a close examination with a 10x hand lens reveals dark, olive-brown, club-shaped, muriform (longitudinal and transverse septa) multi-celled conidia (120-296 x 12-20 um, 8-12 transverse septa, beak up to 3x body length) borne singly or in chains of 2-5 on simple, geniculate conidiophores emerging through stomata on the lower lesion surface. Multiple lesions on a single leaf blade cause widespread necrosis and chlorosis; leaves with 20+ lesions turn yellow, wither, and die prematurely (defoliation progresses upward from the basal canopy in a characteristic gradient). Severely affected potato fields appear brown, 'burnt up', and senescent 2-4 weeks before normal vine kill, reducing tuber bulking time and final tuber dry matter and yield significantly. On stems and petioles, lesions are elongated, slightly sunken, dark brown cankers with faint concentric zonation 5-30 mm long; severe stem cankers on the main stem near the soil line (collar rot) can girdle and kill entire vines. On potato tubers (infection occurring at harvest when tubers are exposed to desiccating vines carrying heavy A. solani sporulation), lesions are superficial to slightly sunken, dark brown to purple-black, circular to irregular, dry, leathery necrotic areas 5-40 mm in diameter with slightly raised, corky margins; when cut, the underlying tuber flesh shows a 1-5 mm deep, firm, dry, dark brown to gray corky necrosis (the rot is firm and dry, distinguishing early blight tuber rot from soft bacterial Erwinia rot or water-soaked late blight tuber rot with reddish-brown granulation). Alternaria solani overwinters as thick-walled, dark, melanized, multi-celled chlamydospores and as dormant mycelium and conidia within infected potato crop debris (stems, leaves, petioles, desiccated vines) on or near the soil surface; it also survives on tomato crop residue, on many wild Solanum weed hosts, and on volunteer potato tubers ('ground keepers' or 'volunteers') that overwinter in the soil and sprout the following spring. In the spring, mature multi-celled conidia are produced abundantly on overwintered crop residue under conditions of alternating wetting/drying cycles and temperatures of 15-30 C; conidia are primarily wind-dispersed (canopy turbulence boundary-layer flow and frontal thunderstorm updrafts carry conidia 5-50 km downwind) and, secondarily, splash-dispersed by rain droplets from residue onto newly emerged lower potato leaves. Infection occurs when a conidium germinates on the leaf surface producing a germ tube and a melanized appressorium; penetration occurs either directly through the cuticle (most common) or through stomata and hydathodes. Infection requires 6-24 hours of continuous leaf wetness or RH > 90% at optimum temperatures of 24-29 C (75-84 F); the latent period (time from infection to appearance of visible lesions) is 2-8 days depending on temperature and host resistance. A. solani is a polycyclic pathogen with 6-15 repeated secondary cycles per growing season under favorable warm, humid, and periodically wet conditions. Early blight is primarily a 'stress-related' disease: potato plants that are physiologically stressed (old age / senescence, low nitrogen and phosphorus fertility, drought stress, compaction, herbicide injury, insect defoliation by Colorado potato beetle, potato leafhopper, or flea beetle feeding, Verticillium or Fusarium vascular wilt, and virus infection by PVY/PVX/PVA/PLRV) are significantly more susceptible to early blight infection and symptom development than vigorously growing, non-stressed plants; this stress-susceptibility relationship explains why early blight lesions typically appear first on the oldest, senescent basal leaves and why epidemics are often most severe in low-fertility, sandy, drought-prone soils. Management of potato early blight requires an integrated multi-tactic program combining host resistance, cultural practices, predictive forecasting models, and judicious fungicide applications. (1) genetic resistance: polygenic, horizontal, partial quantitative resistance to early blight is present in many advanced potato breeding lines derived from S. tuberosum subsp. andigena, S. phureja, S. microdontum, S. berthaultii, and S. demissum; several commercially important potato cultivars show moderate to good levels of quantitative resistance: 'Atlantic', 'Dakota Diamond', 'Eva', 'MegaChip', 'Snowden', 'Silverton Russet', 'Russet Burbank' (the most widely grown processing potato in North America, moderately susceptible but not highly susceptible). 'Red Pontiac', 'Red Norland', 'Yukon Gold', 'Kennebec' are highly susceptible and require intensive fungicide programs in early-blight-prone areas. Several major dominant gene EB-resistant loci (EB1, EB2, EB3) have been mapped in diploid S. chacoense and S. berthaultii and are being introgressed into tetraploid S. tuberosum via marker-assisted breeding. (2) cultural practices: (a) 2-4 year crop rotations with non-Solanaceous crops (corn, small grains, soybean, alfalfa, sugarbeet) to reduce soil-surface debris-borne inoculum levels; avoid following potato with tomato or eggplant. (b) tillage: incorporate and deeply bury potato vine residue with a moldboard plow in the fall after harvest rather than leaving chopped vines on the soil surface; this reduces the following spring's A. solani primary inoculum by 50-80%. (c) fertility: maintain adequate balanced nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and micronutrient (Mn, Zn) fertility; apply split-nitrogen applications to avoid late-season N deficiency-induced plant senescence and stress; avoid excessive late-season N which promotes succulent growth and delays maturity. (d) irrigation: maintain optimal soil moisture using deficit-irrigation scheduling; avoid both over-irrigation (prolonged leaf wetness) and severe drought stress. (e) pest and stress management: implement effective programs for Colorado potato beetle, potato leafhopper, flea beetle, Verticillium wilt, and PVY virus to prevent additional physiological stress that predisposes plants to early blight. (f) vine-kill timing: chemically or mechanically desiccate vines 2-3 weeks prior to harvest to reduce A. solani sporulation on vines and minimize tuber contact with inoculum-bearing vine debris during mechanical harvesting operations. (3) predictive forecasting and disease-warning systems are widely used for potato early blight to schedule fungicide applications only when infection risk exceeds action thresholds. The most extensively validated model is the TOM-CAST / Epi-Blight model (originally developed for tomato A. solani, adapted for potato by Michigan State University and the University of Wisconsin) which calculates daily physiological time (P-day) units based on leaf wetness duration, average temperature during wet periods, and plant age / growth stage; initial fungicide sprays are triggered at P-day = 300-400 depending on cultivar resistance level, with subsequent sprays scheduled based on accumulated P-days and rain events. TOM-CAST-based spray programs reduce total fungicide use by 25-50% compared to calendar-based weekly or 7-day protectant programs while maintaining equivalent early blight control. (4) chemical fungicide programs are the primary management tool for early blight control in commercial potato production in high-yield-loss-risk areas. The most effective fungicide groups in Wisconsin / USDA / Cornell potato IPM trials are: FRAC M3 multi-site contact protectant (mancozeb, maneb, metiram, chlorothalonil; backbone protectant materials with zero resistance risk, used as tank-mix partners with all single-site fungicides). FRAC 3 DMI triazoles (difenoconazole, propiconazole, tebuconazole, prothioconazole, tetraconazole, metconazole; good protectant + 2-4 day curative kickback activity against leaf infection; FRAC 3 resistance risk is moderate in A. solani; reduced sensitivity populations are documented in the Columbia Basin and central US since 2010). FRAC 7 SDHI (boscalid, fluxapyroxad, penthiopyrad, benzovindiflupyr, pydiflumetofen, solatenol + pyraclostrobin premixes; excellent protectant + mild systemic activity against both foliar and tuber early blight; A. solani SDHI-resistant populations (conferring 2-5x EC50 shift) are reported in Idaho, Washington, and Ontario; always tank-mix SDHI with full-rate multi-site FRAC M3). FRAC 11 QoI (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, trifloxystrobin, famoxadone; good protectant + limited translaminar movement; QoI resistance is extremely widespread in A. solani globally since the mid-2000s due to the F129L mutation in Cyt b gene - QoI-alone sprays are now largely ineffective in most potato-growing regions; QoI must always be tank-mixed with multi-site and alternated with non-QoI FRAC groups when used). FRAC 9+12 AP + anilino-pyrimidine (cyprodinil + fludioxonil; good protectant activity against tuber infection and foliar blight). FRAC U6 (fluopyram; excellent SDHI-like activity with different cross-resistance pattern to FRAC 7). FRAC 50 (cyflufenamid, metrafenone; moderate protectant control). All fungicide programs must follow strict FRAC resistance management guidelines: limit maximum 2-3 consecutive applications of any single FRAC group before switching to a different mode of action; always tank-mix a full recommended labeled rate of multi-site FRAC M3 partner with every single-site fungicide application; do not apply more than 4-5 applications per season of any high-risk FRAC group (FRAC 7, FRAC 11, FRAC 3). Organic potato production early blight control programs rely on FRAC M1 copper (Bordeaux mixture, copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, tribasic copper sulfate), copper + elemental sulfur combinations, potassium bicarbonate, Bacillus amyloliquefaciens QST 713, B. subtilis GB03, Streptomyces lydicus WYEC 108, Reynoutria sachalinensis extract, and neem oil applied on 7-10 day protectant schedules initiated at first lesion appearance; these organic programs typically achieve 40-70% early blight reduction under moderate disease pressure compared to the best conventional programs, and are usually not sufficient for commercial production of highly susceptible cultivars like 'Red Norland' or 'Yukon Gold' in high-pressure years. (5) post-harvest tuber storage management: ensure potato tubers are surface-dry before storage; cure tubers at 10-13 C (50-55 F) and 95% RH for 10-14 days immediately after harvest to promote periderm suberization and wound healing which limits development of new early blight tuber lesion expansion during storage; maintain cool storage temperatures of 3-6 C (37-43 F) for table-stock and chip-processing potatoes; remove and grade out any tubers showing visible early blight lesions before placing into long-term storage.
